title: Nicomachean Ethics
author: Aristotle
openingChapterLabel: Book I — The Good for Man
openingText: Every art and every systematic branch of knowledge, along with every action and deliberate choice, seems to aim at some good. This is why people often describe the highest good as "that at which all things aim."
about:
The Nicomachean Ethics asks how human beings can live well. Aristotle examines happiness, character, choice, pleasure, friendship, and the relationship between intellectual and moral virtues. Its central concept, eudaimonia, is commonly translated as happiness or flourishing. Aristotle understands it as activity in accordance with virtue over a complete life, rather than merely a passing feeling.

Books I–II establish the framework: happiness, the doctrine of the mean, and the development of moral virtue through habituation. Books III–V examine voluntary action, choice, and the individual moral virtues, including justice. Book VI treats the intellectual virtues. Book VII examines self-control, lack of self-control, and pleasure. The two books VIII–IX concern friendship. Book X returns to pleasure and happiness and presents contemplation as the highest activity.

The work connects the question of right action with the question of what kind of person to become. It also reflects ancient assumptions about gender, slavery, and society that invite critical examination.

angleCards.title: Flourishing, not happiness.
angleCards.text: The word we translate as happiness — eudaimonia — does not mean a feeling. It means a life fully lived, in the exercise of distinctively human capacities. Aristotle's answer to "what should I want?" is more demanding and more interesting than modern self-help's version of the same question.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand eudaimonia as Aristotle meant it — not subjective happiness but the objective activity of living well — and see what that demands of a person across a lifetime.

angleCards.title: The mean between excess and deficiency.
angleCards.text: Courage stands between cowardice and recklessness; generosity between miserliness and wastefulness. Aristotle describes many moral virtues through excess and deficiency. The mean is the response appropriate to the person and circumstances, rather than a mechanical midpoint.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the doctrine of the mean through Aristotle's catalogue of virtues — and ask whether this framework actually tracks the moral reality of specific virtues or whether it strains under the weight of some of them.

angleCards.title: Friendship as the heart of a good life.
angleCards.text: Two books out of ten are on friendship. Aristotle believes no one would choose to live without friends, even with every other good. He distinguishes friendships of utility, pleasure, and virtue — and argues that the third kind, built on mutual admiration of character, is both rare and constitutive of who we become.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Nicomachean Ethics primarily through its treatment of friendship — what Aristotle thinks genuine friendship requires, why he gives it so much weight, and whether his three-tier distinction holds up.

angleCards.title: Practical wisdom as the master virtue.
angleCards.text: Phronesis—practical wisdom—is the capacity to deliberate and judge well about action. It requires experience and attention to particulars; general rules alone are insufficient. Aristotle connects it closely with moral virtue and insists that ethical inquiry should help us become good, not merely knowledgeable.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the role of phronesis across the Ethics — how Aristotle distinguishes practical from theoretical knowledge, and what it means that good character cannot be reduced to following principles.

cast.name: Eudaimonia
cast.description: The highest human good, understood as activity in accordance with virtue over a complete life. Aristotle considers how character, friends, resources, and good or bad fortune affect our ability to live well. His emphasis on a complete life does not mean that we can call someone happy only after death.

cast.name: The Golden Mean
cast.description: Many moral virtues are described as a mean between excess and deficiency: courage between recklessness and cowardice, generosity between wastefulness and miserliness, truthfulness between boastfulness and self-deprecation. The mean varies with the person and circumstances and requires judgment. Justice receives a distinct and more complex treatment.

cast.name: Practical Wisdom (Phronesis)
cast.description: The intellectual virtue concerned with deliberating well about what benefits human life as a whole. It requires general understanding and experience of particulars. Practical wisdom and moral virtue depend on each other: choosing good ends and reasoning well about action must go together.

cast.name: Friendship (Philia)
cast.description: Aristotle devotes Books VIII and IX to friendship, broadly understood to include relationships between friends, relatives, and fellow citizens. He distinguishes friendships based on utility, pleasure, and good character. In complete friendship, friends wish each other well for the other's own sake; this requires time and a shared life.

cast.name: Virtue (Arete)
cast.description: Not an act but a disposition — a stable, habituated tendency to feel, perceive, and respond in the right way. Virtues are acquired through practice: you become courageous by doing courageous things until courage feels natural rather than effortful. Once formed, they shape what you notice, what you want, and what you find pleasant. The goal is not to control yourself against your inclinations but to become someone whose inclinations are themselves rightly ordered. Aristotle is unsentimental about how long this takes.

cast.name: Contemplation (Theoria)
cast.description: In Book X, Aristotle presents contemplation as the highest activity: especially continuous, self-sufficient, pursued for its own sake, and akin to divine activity. He treats happiness in moral and political activity as secondary. This raises a question about how the different parts of his account of a good life fit together.

whyItMatters.title: Happiness Across a Whole Life
whyItMatters.body: The Ethics asks us to consider more than momentary satisfaction: how we exercise our abilities and how our actions shape a life. Aristotle also recognizes that severe misfortune and a lack of external goods can limit even a good person's opportunities.

whyItMatters.title: Character Develops Through Action
whyItMatters.body: Knowing ethical theory is not enough to make us good. Repeated actions shape habits, feelings, and choices. Aristotle therefore connects ethical understanding with upbringing, practice, and the political arrangements under which people live.

whyItMatters.title: Judgment in Particular Circumstances
whyItMatters.body: It can be difficult to judge when fear is reasonable, how much to give, or how to treat someone justly. The doctrine of the mean and the account of practical wisdom provide a vocabulary for these questions without reducing their answers to a calculation.
